list.listitem: Suspect cocaine use in patients with abnormal mentation, especially in the setting of symptoms of a hyperadrenergic state including nausea, trouble concentrating, anxiety, paranoia, jitteriness, and euphoria. B
A validated screening test for cocaine use disorder is the two-item cocaine screening instrument. B
Initial diagnostic evaluation should include interviewing the patient in a nonjudgmental way and possibly testing for presence of cocaine via urine, saliva, blood, or hair. B
Treatment is primarily supportive with counseling. There is no FDA approved medication available to treat cocaine use disorder. C

background.definition: Cocaine use disorder is a subcategory in DSM-5 under stimulant use disorders. It falls within substance use disorders with 11 diagnostic criteria that combine into a severity of mild, moderate, or severe.

list.listitem: In 2015, 4.8 million people in the United States used cocaine at least once in the previous year; 18.6% of those individuals met DSM-IV diagnostic criteria.

According to data from the CDC WONDER (Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research), drug overdose deaths involving cocaine rose from 6,784 in 2015 to 15,883 in 2019. From 2019 to 2023, cocaine-involved deaths rose 85% to 29,449 deaths.
In the United States in 2016, 855,000 people had a cocaine use disorder in the past year.
It was the first illicit drug used in 0.1% of new illicit drug users in 2013.
One in four adults with ADHD uses cocaine and one in ten develops a stimulant use disorder.

Cocaine use is broadly distributed throughout the United States with higher concentrations in urban areas. According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse’s (NIDA) Community Epidemiology Work Group, cocaine is a major drug of concern in all regions of the country. Specific urban areas with higher use include Miami, Atlanta, Washington, DC, New York City, Minneapolis/St. Paul, San Francisco, Seattle, Denver, and areas of Maine and Texas. Detroit, Denver, New York City, Seattle, and Boston showed statistically significant increases in numbers and rates of cocaine-involved emergency department visits from 2004 to 2007.
Similar to other substance use disorders, cocaine use disorder is a bio-psycho-social illness with characteristic signs and symptoms that are defined in the diagnostic criteria.

Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake pumps of monoamine neurotransmitters in the central and peripheral nervous systems. In addiction, it is believed to act on the cortico-mesolimbic dopamine reward circuit to enhance the dopamine activity.

The two-item screening instrument asks “How many days in the past 12 months have you used drugs other than alcohol?” (positive at 7 or more days) and “How many days in the past 12 months have you used drugs more than you meant to?” (positive at 2 or more days). Although this is most relevant to men who served in the military as it was developed in the VA Primary Care System, it is clinically used in non-VA primary care. A positive to either question is a positive screen and warrants further discussion.B

The USPSTF recommends screening for unhealthy drug use in adults 18 years or older, including pregnant persons, when services for accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and appropriate care can be offered or referred. It found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for unhealthy drug use in adolescents.B
However, a randomized trial (ASPIRE) concluded that adding brief intervention for drug use in primary care does not decrease the mean number of days with problem drug use at 6 months.B
School-based drug abuse prevention programs are ineffective, specifically D.A.R.E., and failed to prevent alcohol use, drug use, or tobacco use.A

The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of primary care-based interventions to prevent illicit drug use in children and young adults. A Cochrane review concluded that evidence is small but has consistent protective effects for interventions designed to prevent or reduce drug use by people under age 25 delivered in school or other settings. There may be some benefit to motivational interviewing and some family interventions.A
Hospitalized patients have a higher prevalence of substance use disorders than the general population. Universal formal screening may increase detection of SUDs and inform treatment decisions.B
Anyone using cocaine recreationally should be considered at risk for addiction. C

Utilization of the 11 diagnostic criteria to diagnose disease along the mild-moderate-severe continuum, including interval reassessment, is valuable in communicating the patient’s current disease state. C

An individual using cocaine at any level is practicing a risky behavior. In order to have a cocaine use disorder, the person would need to have significant psychological impairment or distress. This can manifest itself in many ways, including increasing use against volition, continued use despite having social problems, feelings of craving, and tolerance and withdrawal to non-prescribed stimulants.
Formal diagnostic criteria are defined by the DSM-5.

A pattern of amphetamine-type substance, cocaine, or other stimulant use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, as manifested by at least two of the following, occurring within a 12-month period: The stimulant is often taken in larger amounts or over a longer period than was intended. There is a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down or control stimulant use. A great deal of time is spent in activities necessary to obtain the stimulant, use the stimulant, or recover from its effects. Craving, or a strong desire or urge to use the stimulant. Recurrent stimulant use resulting in a failure to fulfill major role obligations at work, school, or home. Continued stimulant use despite having persistent or recurrent social or interpersonal problems caused or exacerbated by the effects of the stimulant. Important social, occupational, or recreational activities are given up or reduced because of stimulant use. Recurrent stimulant use in situations in which it is physically hazardous. Stimulant use is continued despite knowledge of having a persistent or recurrent physical or psychological problem that is likely to have been caused or exacerbated by the stimulant. Tolerance, as defined by either of the following: A need for markedly increased amounts of the stimulant to achieve intoxication or desired effect. A markedly diminished effect with continued use of the same amount of the stimulant.
Note: This criterion is not considered to be met for those taking stimulant medications solely under appropriate medical supervision, such as medications for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or narcolepsy. Withdrawal, as manifested by either of the following: The characteristic withdrawal syndrome for the stimulant (refer to Criteria A and B of the criteria set for stimulant withdrawal). The stimulant (or a closely related substance) is taken to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms. Note: This criterion is not considered to be met for those taking stimulant medications solely under appropriate medical supervision, such as medications for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or narcolepsy. Specify if: In early remission: After full criteria for stimulant use disorder were previously met, none of the criteria for stimulant use disorder have been met for at least 3 months but for less than 12 months (with the exception that Criterion A4, “Craving, or a strong desire or urge to use the stimulant,” may be met). In sustained remission: After full criteria for stimulant use disorder were previously met, none of the criteria for stimulant use disorder have been met at any time during a period of 12 months or longer (with the exception that Criterion A4, “Craving, or a strong desire or urge to use the stimulant,” may be met). Specify if: In a controlled environment: This additional specifier is used if the individual is in an environment where access to stimulants is restricted.
A focused history includes the onset of use, duration of use, quantity, frequency, any previous periods of recovery, and mode of use.
Cocaine can be used as a powder and insufflated, as a solid, crack, and smoked or dissolved and injected. It is relatively difficult to dissolve, making this route the least common.

The various routes of use have different sequela. Insufflation can lead to nose bleeds, septal perforation, and septal collapse. Injection can result in all the infectious sequela of injection drug use, including HCV, HIV, bacterial infection, and bacterial endocarditis.

Assess use of all substances of misuse, both past and current, including both illegal and pharmaceutical-grade substances. Ask about the duration, quantity, frequency, route, and any periods of recovery. Also ask about any family history of substance use disorder and other behavioral health concerns.

The physical exam should be tailored to the patient’s route of use and also include a general full physical as many patients may not have recent or regular access to healthcare. Stigmata of disease include skin lesions from injection, perforated septum from insufflation, and nosebleed. “Crack lip” and “crack thumb” are related to heat injuries.
Evidence of subcutaneous injection include salmon-colored marks on the skin and areas of infection and skin slough.
Skin picking or scratching can be associated with cocaine use, though it is more common with methamphetamine use.
Tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, tremulousness, and diaphoresis can all be seen.
Psychiatric concerns can include extreme agitation and irritability/mood lability (including depression and suicidality).
Cocaine with levamisole, a common agent contaminating cocaine supply, can cause agranulocytosis and other hematologic disorders, skin necrosis, and symptoms consistent with pulmonary hypertension.
Loss of consciousness may occur due to cocaine-induced seizures or stroke.
Perform a neurological exam as cocaine can result in weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, visual field deficit, and ataxia.

Most people in substance use treatment will have urine drug testing performed both for diagnosis and monitoring. This can sometimes reveal other substances of misuse. Hair, nails, saliva and blood testing can also be done.

Urine can be used to determine what is present to narrow the substance of misuse. It is important to remember that a point-of-care urine drug test is a screening test and may need confirmatory testing by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry if not endorsed by the patient or otherwise has spurious results.

Each route of testing has different detection windows. It is important to know how to interpret each of these tests. Local laboratories and Medical Review Officers can be of assistance as each region and lab may be slightly different.

In individuals presenting with high blood pressure, sweating, headache, tachycardia, tremors, anxiety and weight loss, urinary catecholamines and a CT of the abdomen should be considered to rule out pheochromocytoma.
In individuals with chest pain, order an EKG and cardiac enzymes, as cocaine intoxication can cause vasoconstriction resulting in a myocardial infarction.
In individuals with seizures or focal neurological symptoms, order a CT, MRI, or EEG to rule out intracranial causes such as stroke.
In individuals with tachycardia, hyperactivity, and/or weight loss, order a T4 and TSH to rule out thyrotoxicosis.

As cocaine use is associated with an increased risk of blood-borne and sexually transmitted diseases, order tests for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, and be alert for possible disease complications of these conditions.
Note that synthetic cannabinoids and cathinone derivatives are not detected by urine testing and may warrant further investigation if no cause is found on work up.

As cocaine is often contaminated with levamisole, a CBC for possible anemia and agranulocytosis may be indicated in individuals presenting with stigmata of anemia such as pallor, weakness, and lethargy.
Consider cocaine use in patients presenting with abnormal mentation.
The initial evaluation should include evaluation for symptoms of a hyperadrenergic state including nausea, trouble concentrating, anxiety, paranoia, jitteriness, and euphoria.
Complications of cocaine can include acute MI, seizures, stroke, agranulocytosis (from levamisole contamination), and suicidality.
Many psychological sequelae exist for individuals with cocaine use including family disruption, work impairment, financial loss, violent behavior, paranoia, and suicidality.
Patients should be referred for evaluation by an addiction specialty physician and offered evaluation by a licensed therapy provider.
Behavioral therapies are the mainstay of treatment for cocaine use disorders. Effective behavioral therapies include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and contingency management (CM). C

There are no FDA-approved medications for the treatment of cocaine use disorders. Many clinical trials have found a limited benefit for some medications, but there are no medications that have been found to be consistently effective for the treatment of cocaine use disorders. B
Patients who are using cocaine and seek treatment have high rates of psychiatric comorbidity. Consider referring patients who use cocaine to an addiction specialist. C

Stimulants: A Cochrane Review of psychostimulant drugs for cocaine dependence concluded that they could provide some improvement in abstinence, but no effect on treatment retention. It also concluded that substitution treatment using other stimulants to replace cocaine deserves further study.

Anticonvulsants: Cochrane Reviews found no evidence supporting the effectiveness of carbamazepine specifically, or anticonvulsants, as a category for cocaine dependence. There is similarly no evidence of benefit for vigatrabin or dopamine agonists.

Topiramate: Although small randomized trials have shown a benefit of topiramate for cocaine dependence, a systematic review and meta-analysis did not find evidence of benefit for topiramate on treatment retention in cocaine use disorder.

Disulfiram: A Cochrane Review found limited evidence to support the use of disulfiram for cocaine dependence. Subsequent studies have not shown a benefit of disulfiram when added to behavioral therapies, and also suggest that disulfiram may be less beneficial in women.

Modafinil: A double-blind placebo-controlled 8-week trial of 94 cocaine dependent volunteers found that modafinil increased cocaine abstinence during the last 3 weeks of the trial, (23% vs. 9%). Modafinil-treated subjects had statistically significant decreases in craving and felt subjectively “very much improved” to a greater degree than placebo-treated subjects. However, a subsequent systematic review of 11 studies with 876 participants found that modafinil overall was no more effective than placebo at improving retention in treatment or achieving remission from cocaine use disorder as indicated by negative urine toxicology screening.
Antidepressants and antipsychotics, based on 2 Cochrane reviews, demonstrate no clear evidence of efficacy for cocaine dependence.
Auricular acupuncture was found to be no more effective than placebo needle insertion or relaxation therapy in reducing cocaine use among cocaine dependent adults.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a psychotherapeutic treatment that helps patients understand thoughts and feelings that influence behavior. CBT helps prevent relapse through assisting patients with the development of skills that support abstinence. These skills include recognition of situations in which relapse may occur, and coping with problems that might result in drug use. CBT can be used alone or in conjunction with other therapies. In addition to in-person CBT training, computer-based interventions have also shown a benefit in reducing drug use.

Contingency management (CM) programs provide motivational incentives for patients who abstain from drug use. Typically, patients receive “points” (e.g., chips, vouchers) for drug-free urines, which can be exchanged for pro-social rewards that encourage healthy lifestyles. CM can be combined with other treatments, and is particularly useful in supporting early recovery.

Residential treatment are sober living environments where patients with substance use disorders provide mutual support to assist in recovery. Residential treatment often takes place over many months, and typically includes services that focus on employment, mental health, and other types of support. Specific evidence for the benefit of residential treatment in cocaine use disorders is lacking. In general, there is evidence for decreased drug use among patients in residential treatment, but long-term outcomes are not well studied. However, a Cochrane Review did not find a benefit for treatment collaboratives over other forms of residential drug treatment.

Psychosocial interventions to reduce parental substance misuse, especially heroin, cocaine, and alcohol, appear moderately effective in reducing alcohol and drug use, based on a Cochrane review. The most promise involves use of integrated psychosocial interventions combining parenting skills with substance use management.

Citicoline: A double-blind, 12-week RCT of 130 patients with bipolar I disorder and cocaine dependence showed transient decreased cocaine use in those treated with the dietary supplement citicoline. Between-group differences in cocaine uses arose early in the study, but were significantly attenuated by the end of the trial. Over the course of the trial, the number of cocaine abstainers did not significantly differ between the two groups (placebo 19.7% vs. citicoline 23%).

Limited studies have investigated neurostimulation techniques, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation, for cocaine use disorders. The literature so far does not support the efficacy of these approaches.
Substance use disorders tend to be chronic recurring conditions and benefit from prolonged treatment.

Observational epidemiological data suggest that the transition from cocaine use to dependence occurs in 21% of individuals, and occurs on an average of 4 years after the onset of use. These estimates are obtained from the first and second wave of national epidemiologic data in the United States.B

Cardiovascular effects are the most severe complications of cocaine use, including arrhythmias, acute coronary syndromes, and sudden-cardiac death. Severe neurologic consequences of cocaine use include cerebrovascular accidents and coma.B

Regular use of cocaine may lead to tolerance and the need to use cocaine at increasing dosages or more frequently to alleviate withdrawal or induce euphoria. Sensitization may also occur through regular use of cocaine, resulting in anxiety, seizures, and paranoia.C

Patients who are receiving treatment for cocaine use disorders typically have urine drug testing for cocaine metabolites monitored periodically during the course of treatment. There are no evidence-based guidelines that address the frequency or duration of monitoring. C
Cocaine is not a structural teratogen.
Cocaine use during pregnancy is associated with premature rupture of membranes and a number of other placenta-associated syndromes (e.g., placental abruption, placental infarction, and preeclampsia).
It is also associated with preterm birth, intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age infants.

Prenatal cocaine exposure is associated with a number of adverse behavioral outcomes through early adolescence and adulthood. These associations include poorer perceptual organization, lower IQ, visual-spatial information processing deficits, and problems with attention, language, executive function, and behavior regulation.

Onset of cocaine use in adolescence is associated with greater neurocognitive impairments relative to controls and is associated with a greater frequency of polydrug use when compared to adult-onset cocaine users.
